# Overview {#sec-overview}

The radial depth of cut ($a_e$) is a process parameter that is not
directly measurable during flat milling, yet it governs the
instantaneous chip load and, through the Kienzle cutting-force model,
the torque-generating current drawn by the spindle motor. This work
estimates $a_e$ (expressed as the engagement ratio $a_e/D$, where $D$ is
the tool diameter) from the spindle motor current signal using a
Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) operating on a vector of physics-informed
features rather than on the raw time-series. The feature vector is
constructed so that each entry has an explicit interpretation under the
Kienzle model, which allows the data-driven prediction to be
cross-checked against the underlying cutting mechanics rather than
treated as a black-box regression. Two complementary search strategies,
an exhaustive Grid Search and a Bayesian Tree-structured Parzen
Estimator (TPE), are applied to the coupled hyperparameter space of
network depth, layer width, dropout rate, and signal segmentation, and
their outcomes are compared under identical training conditions. The
remainder of this section describes the experimental data, the signal
pre-processing and feature-extraction pipeline, the network architecture
and training procedure, the two hyperparameter optimisation strategies,
and the Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout scheme used for uncertainty
quantification. The physical model underlying the Kienzle-normalised
features of @sec-features, namely the specific cutting force, the
cutting torque, and its conversion to the measured spindle current, is
developed first in @sec-kienzle.

# Kienzle Cutting-Force Model: Formulation and Development {#sec-kienzle}

The Kienzle approach describes the specific cutting force $k_c$, i.e.
the cutting force per unit chip cross-sectional area, as a power-law
function of the chip thickness $h$,

$$k_c(h) = k_{c1.1} \cdot h^{-m_c},
\tag{1}$$

where $k_{c1.1}$ is the specific cutting force at the reference chip
thickness $h = 1\,\text{mm}$, and $m_c$ is the material-dependent slope
of the force–thickness relationship on a logarithmic scale. Both
$k_{c1.1}$ (in $\text{N}/\text{mm}^2$) and $m_c$ (dimensionless) are
empirical material constants, identified for the workpiece material in
the companion Bayesian parameter-identification study and used here as
fixed nominal values $k_{c1.1}^{\text{nom}}$, $m_c^{\text{nom}}$. The
power-law form in eq. 1 captures the size effect observed in metal
cutting, whereby the specific cutting force increases as the chip
thickness decreases, and provides the link between the geometric cutting
conditions and the resulting force that the remainder of this section
exploits.

In flat-end milling with $z$ teeth, the chip thickness is not constant
but varies with the angular position $\varphi_i$ of each tooth $i$ as it
sweeps through the workpiece. For a feed per tooth $f_z$, the
instantaneous chip thickness of tooth $i$ is

$$h_i(\varphi_i) = f_z \sin\varphi_i,
\tag{2}$$

which vanishes at the entry and exit of the cut
($\varphi_i \in \{0, \pi\}$) and is maximal at $\varphi_i = \pi/2$.
Combining eq. 1 and eq. 2, and taking the chip width equal to the axial
depth of cut $a_p$ (for a cutting-edge angle $\kappa = 90^\circ$), the
tangential cutting force contributed by tooth $i$ is

$$F_{c,i}(\varphi_i) = k_c\big(h_i(\varphi_i)\big) \cdot a_p \cdot h_i(\varphi_i)
= k_{c1.1} \cdot a_p \cdot f_z^{\,1-m_c} \cdot \big(\sin\varphi_i\big)^{1-m_c}.
\tag{3}$$

Equation 3 expresses the cutting force on a single tooth entirely in
terms of the cutting parameters $a_p$, $f_z$, the Kienzle constants
$k_{c1.1}$, $m_c$, and the instantaneous engagement angle $\varphi_i$,
and is the form referenced directly by the Kienzle-normalised feature of
@sec-features.

The angular position of tooth $i$ at time $t$ follows from the spindle
angular speed $\omega$ and the angular offset of $2\pi/z$ between
consecutive teeth,

$$\varphi_i(t) = \big(\varphi_0 + \omega t - (i-1)\tfrac{2\pi}{z}\big) \bmod 2\pi,
\qquad i = 1, \dots, z,
\tag{4}$$

where $\varphi_0$ is the initial angular offset. A tooth contributes to
the cutting torque only while it is engaged with the workpiece, i.e.
while $\varphi_i(t)$ lies within the engagement window
$[\varphi_{\text{in}}, \varphi_{\text{out}}]$. The width of this window
is set by the radial depth of cut $a_e$ relative to the tool diameter
$D$: for a given exit angle $\varphi_{\text{out}}$, the entry angle
follows from the peripheral-milling engagement geometry as

$$\varphi_{\text{in}} = \varphi_{\text{out}} - \arccos\!\left(1 - \frac{2a_e}{D}\right).
\tag{5}$$

Equation 5 is the link between the radial engagement ratio $a_e/D$, the
unobserved quantity of interest in this work, and the fraction of each
revolution during which the cutting force in eq. 3 is non-zero. A larger
$a_e/D$ widens the engagement window, increases the number of teeth in
cut at any instant, and raises the average cutting torque, which is the
mechanism the Kienzle-normalised and tooth-passing features of
@sec-features are designed to capture.

Summing the contributions of all engaged teeth and converting from force
to torque via the tool radius $D/2$ gives the total cutting torque at
time $t$,

$$M_c(t) = \frac{D}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{z} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\varphi_i(t) \in
[\varphi_{\text{in}}, \varphi_{\text{out}}]\right] \cdot F_{c,i}\big(\varphi_i(t)\big),
\tag{6}$$

with $\mathbb{1}[\cdot]$ the indicator function and $\varphi_i(t)$,
$F_{c,i}$ given by eq. 4 and eq. 3 respectively. $M_c(t)$ is the
quantity simulated by the `torque_time_series` method of `KienzleModel`
and is the noise-free physical counterpart of the measured spindle
signal.

The spindle drive does not output torque directly; it outputs the
torque-generating current $I_q(t)$, related to $M_c(t)$ through the
motor torque constant $k_m$ (in $\text{N}\!\cdot\!\text{mm}/\text{A}$),
with an additive no-load (friction) offset $\bar{I}_{\text{frict}}$
representing the current drawn to overcome spindle and drivetrain
friction in the absence of cutting,

$$I_q(t) = \frac{M_c(t)}{k_m} + \bar{I}_{\text{frict}}.
\tag{7}$$

Equation 7 is implemented in `current_time_series` as $M_c(t)/k_m$, with
$\bar{I}_{\text{frict}}$ measured separately during a spindle-idle
window and added back when generating synthetic signals or, conversely,
subtracted from measured signals during the no-load correction of eq. 8.
Together, eq. 1 through eq. 7 define the forward map from the cutting
parameters $(a_p, f_z, D, z, a_e, \omega)$ and the Kienzle constants
$(k_{c1.1}, m_c)$ to the measured spindle current, and form the physical
basis against which the data-driven features of @sec-features and the
Bayesian parameter identification of the companion study are both
interpreted.

# Experimental Data {#sec-data}

The dataset comprises 64 flat-milling measurement files acquired on a
Siemens SINUMERIK machine tool and exported in SinuTrace CSV format.
Each file contains the torque-generating spindle current as a time
series, sampled at frequency $f_s$, together with the corresponding
cutting parameters: axial depth of cut $a_p$, feed per tooth $f_z$, tool
diameter $D$, number of teeth $z$, and spindle speed $n$ (rpm). Cutting
parameters and per-experiment metadata are stored separately from the
signal data, in tables denoted `cut_param` and `df_info`, and are joined
to each measurement by experiment index during dataset construction. The
nominal Kienzle constants for the workpiece material,
$k_{c1.1}^{\text{nom}}$ and $m_c^{\text{nom}}$, are taken from the
materials database used in the companion Bayesian
parameter-identification study and serve as fixed reference values for
the physics-informed normalisation described in @sec-features.

# Signal Pre-Processing and Segmentation {#sec-preprocessing}

Before feature extraction, each raw current signal $I(t)$ is corrected
for the no-load (friction) baseline by subtracting the mean idle current
$\bar{I}_{\text{frict}}$ measured prior to tool engagement,

$$I_c(t) = I(t) - \bar{I}_{\text{frict}}.
\tag{8}$$

The initial ramp-up interval, during which the spindle accelerates to
the commanded speed and the tool has not yet reached steady-state
engagement, is discarded. The remaining signal is then divided into
$N_{\text{seg}}$ contiguous, equal-length segments,

$$I_c(t) \;\longrightarrow\; \{I_c^{(1)}, I_c^{(2)}, \dots, I_c^{(N_{\text{seg}})}\},
\qquad
|I_c^{(j)}| = \left\lfloor \frac{|I_c|}{N_{\text{seg}}} \right\rfloor,
\tag{9}$$

each segment inheriting the cutting parameters of its parent
measurement. Segmentation serves two purposes: it multiplies the number
of training samples (e.g. $N_{\text{seg}}=4$ expands the dataset from 64
to 256 samples), and it exposes the model to localised variations in
engagement within a single pass. $N_{\text{seg}}$ is itself treated as a
hyperparameter in @sec-hpo, since the optimal segmentation length
carries a physical interpretation tied to the tooth-engagement phases of
the milling cycle.

# Physics-Informed Feature Extraction {#sec-features}

For each segment $I_c^{(j)}$, a fixed-length feature vector
$\mathbf{x} \in
\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is constructed. The features fall into three groups:
global statistical descriptors, per-revolution torque-proxy statistics,
and spectral and Kienzle-normalised descriptors that embed the
cutting-force model directly into the feature space.

## Statistical Descriptors

The root-mean-square value, peak amplitude, crest factor, mean rectified
value, and standard deviation of the segment are computed as

$$\text{RMS} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} I_c(t)^2}, \qquad
\text{peak} = \max_t |I_c(t)|, \qquad
\text{crest} = \frac{\text{peak}}{\text{RMS} + \varepsilon},
\tag{10}$$

where $T$ is the segment length in samples and $\varepsilon = 10^{-9}$
prevents division by zero on a silent signal.

## Per-Revolution Torque Proxy

The segment is partitioned into complete spindle revolutions of length
$T_{\text{rev}} = \lfloor f_s \cdot 60 / n \rfloor$ samples. For each
revolution $k$, the mean and maximum current are computed as $\bar{I}_k$
and $I_{\max,k}$ respectively, giving the revolution-aggregated features

$$\overline{\bar{I}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \bar{I}_k, \qquad
\overline{I_{\max}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} I_{\max,k}, \qquad
\sigma_{I_{\max}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(I_{\max,k} -
\overline{I_{\max}}\right)^2},
\tag{11}$$

with $K$ the number of complete revolutions in the segment. The
per-revolution maximum is directly motivated by the Kienzle model, since
the peak torque per revolution scales with the maximum chip thickness,
which in turn depends on $a_e$ through the tool entry and exit angles.

## Tooth-Passing Band Energy

The tooth-passing frequency is

$$f_{\text{tooth}} = \frac{n}{60} \cdot z \quad \text{[Hz]},
\tag{12}$$

and the spectral feature is the fraction of total signal energy
contained in a $\pm 50\,\text{Hz}$ band around $f_{\text{tooth}}$,

$$E_{\text{tooth}} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{f \in [f_{\text{tooth}}-50,\ f_{\text{tooth}}+50]}
|S(f)|^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{f} |S(f)|^2 + \varepsilon},
\tag{13}$$

where $S(f) = \big|\widehat{I_c}(f)\big|$ is the magnitude spectrum
obtained via the real-valued FFT. Normalising by the total spectral
energy (a Parseval-theorem ratio) renders $E_{\text{tooth}}$ invariant
to the overall signal amplitude. As $a_e$ increases, more material is
engaged per tooth pass, the cutting force modulation at
$f_{\text{tooth}}$ strengthens, and $E_{\text{tooth}}$ increases
monotonically, providing a physically grounded predictor of the
regression target.

## Kienzle-Normalised Torque Residual

The per-tooth cutting force derived in @sec-kienzle (eq. 3) is evaluated
at the nominal Kienzle constants $k_{c1.1}^{\text{nom}}$,
$m_c^{\text{nom}}$ and the commanded cutting parameters $a_p$, $f_z$,
$D$ to obtain a reference torque,

$$M_{c,\text{theory}} = \frac{k_{c1.1}^{\text{nom}} \cdot a_p \cdot f_z^{\,1-m_c^{\text{nom}}}
\cdot D}{2},
\tag{14}$$

and the measured per-revolution mean torque proxy $\overline{\bar{I}}$
(eq. 11) is compared against this reference through the normalised
residual

$$M_{c,\text{norm}} = \frac{\overline{\bar{I}} - M_{c,\text{theory}}}{M_{c,\text{theory}}}.
\tag{15}$$

$M_{c,\text{norm}}$ quantifies the portion of the measured signal that
is not explained by the nominal Kienzle prediction at the commanded
$a_p$ and $f_z$, and is therefore expected to carry the residual
information attributable to the unknown $a_e$. Invalid combinations of
$a_p$ or $f_z$ are guarded against before evaluating eq. 14 to avoid
propagating not-a-number values into the feature matrix.

## Feature Scaling

The complete feature matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$ and
target vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N}$ are standardised
independently using

$$\mathbf{x}'_{i} = \frac{\mathbf{x}_i - \mu_{\mathbf{X}}}{\sigma_{\mathbf{X}}}, \qquad
y'_{i} = \frac{y_i - \mu_{\mathbf{y}}}{\sigma_{\mathbf{y}}},
\tag{16}$$

with $\mu$ and $\sigma$ estimated on the training split only.
Constant-valued columns (e.g. $D$ and $z$ when fixed across all
experiments) are removed prior to scaling via a variance-threshold
filter, since a zero-variance column produces a division by zero under
eq. 16 and propagates not-a-number values to every sample.

# Model Architecture {#sec-model}

The regressor, denoted `AeEstimatorMLP`, is a feed-forward network with
$L$ hidden layers. For input $\mathbf{x}' \in \mathbb{R}^d$, each hidden
layer applies

$$\mathbf{h}^{(l)} = \text{Dropout}_p\Big(\sigma\big(W^{(l)} \mathbf{h}^{(l-1)} +
\mathbf{b}^{(l)}\big)\Big), \qquad l = 1, \dots, L,
\tag{17}$$

with $\mathbf{h}^{(0)} = \mathbf{x}'$, $\sigma(\cdot)$ a ReLU
activation, and a uniform dropout rate $p$ applied after every hidden
layer. The output layer is a single linear unit,
$\hat{y}' = W^{(L+1)}\mathbf{h}^{(L)} + b^{(L+1)}$, producing the
standardised prediction of $a_e/D$. Both the number of layers $L$ and
the per-layer widths $(u_1, \dots, u_L)$ are treated as hyperparameters,
allowing depth and width to vary jointly with the dropout rate $p$.

# Training Procedure {#sec-training}

The network is trained by minimising the Huber loss between the
predicted and measured standardised targets,

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{Huber}}(y', \hat{y}') =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{2}(y' - \hat{y}')^2, & |y' - \hat{y}'| \le \delta, \\[6pt]
\delta\left(|y' - \hat{y}'| - \dfrac{1}{2}\delta\right), & |y' - \hat{y}'| > \delta,
\end{cases}
\tag{18}$$

with $\delta = 1.0$. The Huber loss combines the quadratic behaviour of
mean-squared error for small residuals with the linear behaviour of
mean-absolute error for large residuals, limiting the influence of
outlier segments without discarding them. The network is optimised with
Adam, a batch size of 16, and a fixed budget of 300 training epochs for
all final model evaluations.

# Hyperparameter Optimisation {#sec-hpo}

The hyperparameters $(L, u_1,\dots,u_L, p, N_{\text{seg}})$ jointly
determine model capacity, regularisation strength, and the granularity
of the temporal segmentation described in @sec-preprocessing. Because
these factors interact, an exhaustive Grid Search and a Bayesian TPE
search are run over the same bounded space and compared under identical
training conditions.

## Search Space

The shared search space is defined once, over the number of hidden
layers $L \in
\{1,2,3\}$, a per-layer width drawn from $\{32, 64, 128\}$, a dropout
rate $p \in
\{0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$, and $N_{\text{seg}} \in \{1,2,4,8\}$. One
asymmetry is maintained deliberately between the two strategies: the
Grid Search applies a single uniform width across all $L$ layers,
whereas the TPE sampler searches each layer width independently, since a
uniform-width grid keeps the cardinality of the exhaustive search
tractable while the TPE surrogate can exploit the larger, per-layer
search space without an explosion in trial count.

## Grid Search

The Grid Search evaluates every element of the Cartesian product of the
discretised hyperparameter sets,

$$|\Theta_{\text{grid}}| = |L| \times |u| \times |p| \times |N_{\text{seg}}|,
\tag{19}$$

which for the bounds above yields $3 \times 3 \times 4 \times 4 = 144$
candidate configurations in the default setting. Each configuration is
trained and evaluated on a validation split, and the configuration
minimising $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Huber}}$ on the validation set is
retained. Because eq. 19 grows multiplicatively in the number of
hyperparameters, the Grid Search provides an exhaustive but
computationally expensive reference against which the Bayesian strategy
is benchmarked.

## Bayesian Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator

The TPE sampler, implemented via Optuna, models the hyperparameter space
probabilistically rather than exhaustively. At each trial $t$, the set
of previously evaluated configurations is partitioned into "good" and
"bad" subsets according to a quantile $\gamma$ of the observed
validation losses, and two kernel-density estimates are fitted,

$$\ell(\theta) = p(\theta \mid \mathcal{L}_{\text{Huber}} < \tau), \qquad
g(\theta) = p(\theta \mid \mathcal{L}_{\text{Huber}} \ge \tau),
\tag{20}$$

where $\tau$ is the loss quantile threshold. The next configuration is
drawn to maximise the ratio $\ell(\theta)/g(\theta)$, which is
proportional to the expected improvement over $\tau$. The sampler is
configured with `multivariate=True`, so that $\ell$ and $g$ are fitted
over the joint distribution of all hyperparameters rather than
independently per dimension, which is essential for capturing the
coupling between layer width, depth, and dropout rate. A
`HyperbandPruner` terminates clearly underperforming trials before
completing the full 300-epoch training budget, reducing the wall-clock
cost per trial substantially below that of a complete training run. In
the reported comparison, the Grid Search evaluated 216 configurations
while the TPE sampler reached a comparable or better validation loss
within 80 trials, reflecting the sample efficiency gained from eq. 20
over exhaustive enumeration.

# Uncertainty Quantification via MC Dropout {#sec-mcdropout}

Predictive uncertainty is estimated using Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout. At
inference time, dropout (eq. 17) is kept active, and $T$ stochastic
forward passes are performed for a given input $\mathbf{x}'$, yielding
predictions $\{\hat{y}'_1, \dots, \hat{y}'_T\}$. The predictive mean and
variance are

$$\hat{\mu}(\mathbf{x}') = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\hat{y}'_t, \qquad
\hat{\sigma}^2(\mathbf{x}') = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\hat{y}'_t -
\hat{\mu}(\mathbf{x}')\right)^2.
\tag{21}$$

$\hat{\sigma}^2(\mathbf{x}')$ approximates the epistemic uncertainty of
the model at $\mathbf{x}'$ and is reported alongside
$\hat{\mu}(\mathbf{x}')$ for both the Grid Search and TPE best
configurations, allowing the two optimisation strategies to be compared
not only on point-prediction accuracy but also on the sharpness of their
predictive distributions.

# Workflow Summary {#sec-workflow}

The complete data pipeline proceeds from raw acquisition to model
selection in six stages: (1) loading of the 64 SinuTrace measurement
files together with their cutting parameters from `cut_param` and
`df_info`; (2) friction-baseline correction, ramp-up removal, and
segmentation into $N_{\text{seg}}$ parts per eq. 8–9; (3) extraction of
the physics-informed feature vector per eq. 10–15, combining
statistical, per-revolution, spectral, and Kienzle-normalised
descriptors; (4) standardisation of features and targets per eq. 16,
with zero-variance columns removed beforehand; (5) joint optimisation of
network architecture, dropout, and segmentation via Grid Search (eq. 19)
and Bayesian TPE (eq. 20) under the shared training procedure of eq. 18;
and (6) final retraining of both selected configurations at the full
300-epoch budget, followed by MC Dropout evaluation (eq. 21) for
predictive accuracy and uncertainty comparison. All physics-related
computations, namely the Kienzle force evaluation and the
signal-processing utilities used in stages 2 and 3, are delegated to the
shared `KienzleModel` and `MillingSignalUtils` classes used throughout
the companion Bayesian parameter-identification study, ensuring that the
physical model underlying both research threads remains a single,
consistently maintained implementation.
